issues.legal_issue: Coal particles discharged from a coal washery and deposited elsewhere remain coal and constitute a mineral.
material_facts: Small coal particles escaped from coal washeries with water and accumulated in storage ponds, river beds, and on land.
The deposited material retained its carbonaceous character and coal elements.
The collected material was made into briquettes and used as fuel.
issues.conclusion: The slurry was coal in liquid form and continued to be coal and a mineral after it was deposited.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the meaning of slurry as a liquid mixture, considered coal’s character and use, and approved the reasoning in Kesari Mal Jain v. State of Bihar that carbonaceous particles discharged from a coal washery and used as fuel are coal. Coal is specified as a mineral in the First Schedule to the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.

rule.if: classification_dispute_involves_washery_slurry and coal_particles_escape_with_water and deposited_material_retains_coal_character and deposited_material_is_recovered_for_fuel

predicates.classification_dispute_involves_washery_: The dispute concerns the classification of material discharged from a coal washery.
predicates.coal_particles_escape_with_water: Coal particles leave a washery mixed with discharged water.
predicates.deposited_material_retains_coal_characte: The material deposited after discharge retains the carbonaceous character of coal.
predicates.deposited_material_is_recovered_for_fuel: The deposited material is recovered and used as fuel.

issues.definition: When a classification dispute concerns washery slurry, the slurry remains coal and a mineral if coal particles escape with water, retain coal character after deposit, and are recovered for fuel.

issues.legal_issue: The parliamentary declaration covering regulation of mines and mineral development includes regulation of coal-mine slurry disposal, and the absence of central rules does not restore state legislative competence over that subject.
material_facts: The slurry contained coal particles and was discharged from coal washeries as waste.
The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 declared that the Union would control regulation of mines and development of minerals to the extent provided by the Act.
The Act empowered the Central Government to make rules concerning mineral conservation and disposal or discharge of mine waste.
The Central Government had not made rules specifically regulating the disposal of the slurry.
issues.conclusion: The State Legislature had no legislative competence to regulate the disposal of the slurry; the absence of central rules did not confer such competence on it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 245 and 246 and Entries 23 of List II and 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule, state legislative power over mines and mineral development is subject to parliamentary control. Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, read with Sections 13 and 18, including Section 18(1) and Section 18(2)(k), covers disposal of mine waste. Section 18(1) provides a general rule-making power for conservation and development, while the specified matters in Section 18(2) are illustrative. The Court relied on Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar, Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., and State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone.

rule.if: state_legislative_power_is_contested and parliamentary_control_covers_mine_waste_disposal and central_authority_has_rulemaking_power and central_rules_are_absent

predicates.state_legislative_power_is_contested: A dispute challenges a state's legislative authority over the disposal of material discharged as waste from a mine.
predicates.parliamentary_control_covers_mine_waste_: Parliament has declared Union control over mine and mineral regulation, and the governing law covers disposal of mine waste.
predicates.central_authority_has_rulemaking_power: The governing law gives the central authority power to make rules concerning mineral conservation and mine-waste disposal.
predicates.central_rules_are_absent: The central authority has not made rules specifically governing the disputed mine-waste disposal.

issues.definition: A state legislature lacks power to regulate mine-waste disposal when parliamentary control covers that subject and central rule-making authority exists, even if specific central rules have not been made.

issues.legal_issue: A state government cannot use executive power to regulate or grant rights over a subject from which the state legislature has been excluded by parliamentary control.
material_facts: The State Government granted settlements or leases authorising collection of slurry discharged from coal washeries.
The slurry was mine waste whose disposal fell within the subject controlled by parliamentary legislation.
The State Legislature lacked power to regulate that disposal under the parliamentary declaration and the governing Act.
issues.conclusion: The State Government had no executive authority to grant leases or settlements for collecting the slurry.
issues.legal_principle: Article 162 makes state executive power co-extensive with state legislative power and subject to constitutional and parliamentary limits. Executive action cannot infringe rights where it is unsupported by legislative authority, and the State’s executive power cannot extend into a field taken over by parliamentary legislation. The Court relied on Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Thakur Bharat Singh, and applied Articles 162, 245 and 246, Entry 23 of List II, Entry 54 of List I, and Sections 2 and 18 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.

predicates.challenge_concerns_state_executive_grant: A proceeding challenges a state government's executive grant of rights to collect material discharged as mine waste.
predicates.parliamentary_control_covers_the_subject: Parliamentary legislation covers regulation of the relevant mine-waste disposal.
predicates.state_legislature_lacks_power_over_the_s: The state legislature has been excluded from legislating on the subject covered by parliamentary control.

issues.definition: A state executive grant of collection rights is unauthorised when the subject is covered by parliamentary control and the state legislature lacks power over it.

issues.legal_issue: A state and persons claiming under its leases cannot deny that deposited slurry is a mineral when the state granted those leases on the basis that it was a mineral.
material_facts: The State Government granted leases for collection of slurry and demanded royalty for that collection.
The lease documents treated the deposited material as a mineral and asserted the State’s ownership of it on that basis.
The State and the lessees nevertheless contended that the slurry was not coal or a mineral.
issues.conclusion: It was not open to the State or the lessees to contend that the slurry was not coal or a mineral within the meaning of the governing Act.
issues.legal_principle: A party’s position before the Court cannot depart from the position it adopted in making and relying on the challenged leases. The Court relied on the State’s own lease documents and its treatment of the slurry as a mineral; it applied no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this point.

predicates.challenge_concerns_state_leases_for_slur: A proceeding challenges leases granted by a state for collection of deposited slurry.
predicates.state_leases_treat_deposit_as_mineral: The state grants the leases on the stated basis that the deposited material is a mineral.
predicates.state_or_lessees_deny_mineral_status: The state or persons claiming under the leases later contend that the deposited material is not a mineral.

issues.definition: A state and persons claiming under its leases cannot deny the material’s mineral status when the state granted the leases on the basis that it was a mineral.

issues.legal_issue: A coal washery used to prepare coal for sale is part of a mine, and slurry discharged from it is mine waste.
material_facts: Coal extracted from the mines was crushed and washed to remove impurities and prepare it for sale.
The washeries were used for that ancillary preparation process.
Small coal particles escaped from the washeries in slurry discharged with water.
The parties had treated the slurry as waste from the coal washeries.
issues.conclusion: The washeries were an integral part of the mines, and the slurry discharge was waste arising from operations carried out in a mine and therefore fell within the Act’s coverage of mine-waste disposal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, adopts the meaning of “mine” in Section 2(1)(j) of the Mines Act, 1952. That definition includes premises belonging to a mine where an ancillary process is carried out to prepare minerals or coke for sale. The Court applied that definition with Section 18 of the 1957 Act and also relied on the parties’ consistent position that the slurry was washery waste.

predicates.dispute_concerns_washery_discharge: A dispute concerns material discharged from a coal washery.
predicates.washery_prepares_mined_coal_for_sale: The washery carries out an ancillary process to prepare mined coal for sale.
predicates.discharge_contains_coal_particles: The material discharged from the washery contains particles of coal.

issues.definition: A washery discharge containing coal particles is mine waste when the washery performs an ancillary process preparing mined coal for sale.

issues.legal_issue: Land acquired for coal-mining purposes and transferred to a coal-mining company remains that company’s land for purposes of challenging a state grant to collect slurry from it.
material_facts: The disputed plot was expressly included in notifications issued to acquire land and mining rights for coal-related purposes.
The acquired land vested in the Central Government and was transferred to a public coal undertaking.
The appellant company thereafter managed and controlled the relevant coal mines and land.
The respondents produced no material contradicting the company’s title to the plot.
issues.conclusion: The appellant company owned the disputed plot, and the State Government had no authority to grant collection rights over slurry deposited there.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 4, 7 and 9 of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, under which the land and specified mining rights were acquired and vested before transfer to the coal undertaking. It found the acquisition notifications and subsequent transfer sufficient to establish the company’s ownership.

predicates.challenge_concerns_state_grant_over_acqu: A proceeding challenges a state grant authorising collection of deposited material from land acquired for mining purposes.
predicates.acquisition_includes_the_disputed_land: The acquisition instrument expressly includes the land in dispute.
predicates.acquired_land_is_transferred_to_mining_c: The acquired land is transferred to a company that manages or operates the relevant mines.

issues.definition: A mining company owns land expressly included in a mining-related acquisition and later transferred to it, so a state grant over that land cannot defeat its title.
